/blog/fourteen-agents-one-canvas.title: Why we let 14 agents share one canvas
/blog/fourteen-agents-one-canvas.description: Queues are slow and handoffs lose context. Here is how claiming layers lets a crew build in parallel without stepping on each other.
h1: Why we let 14 agents share one canvas
p: Queues are slow and handoffs lose context. Here is how claiming layers lets a crew build in parallel without stepping on each other.
Our first prototype had one agent doing everything, in order. It worked, and it took eleven minutes for a landing page. Splitting the work was obvious. Coordinating it was not.

Every layer has one owner at a time. An agent claims a layer by drawing its box, fills it, then releases it. Parents are always claimed before their children, so nobody types into a frame that does not exist yet.
Fourteen turned out to be the sweet spot. Fewer agents leave the canvas idle. More agents spend their time waiting on parents instead of building.

/blog/prompts-are-layouts.description: A good prompt is closer to a grid than a paragraph. Why constraints make AI output feel designed instead of generated.
h1: Prompts are layouts: designing with constraints
h2: Constraints are taste you can write down
p: A good prompt is closer to a grid than a paragraph. Why constraints make AI output feel designed instead of generated.

Generated sites often look generated for one reason: nothing was ruled out. Give the swarm a 4px spacing rhythm, one typeface pair and a 1200px content width, and the results start to feel considered.
Designers carry rules in their heads. Writing them into the brief lets every agent follow the same rules, which is what makes fourteen contributors look like one designer.
Our favourite constraint is the boring one: a maximum of two font sizes per section. It removes more noise than any style prompt.

/blog/how-to-write-a-brief.title: How to write a brief the swarm can build from
/blog/how-to-write-a-brief.description: Agents are fast, not psychic. The five lines that turn a vague idea into a site you would actually ship.
h1: How to write a brief the swarm can build from
h2: Name the job, not the vibe
p: Agents are fast, not psychic. The five lines that turn a vague idea into a site you would actually ship.

Every build starts with a brief, and most briefs are too polite. “A modern website for my studio” gives fourteen agents nothing to argue with. The best briefs we see are short, specific and a little opinionated.
Start with what the site has to do. Book calls, sell three plans, show forty projects. Scout turns jobs into sections. Adjectives turn into guesses.
Who it is for, in one sentence
The one action a visitor should take
Two or three reference sites you like
One thing you never want to see
That last line matters more than it looks. “No stock photos of handshakes” saves a full round of revisions.
